query: Which method can be used for phase stability, microstructure refinement, and property optimization, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Applying a CALPHAD‐based high-throughput computational screening method can effectively predict phase equilibria, guide microstructure refinement, and optimize properties in high-entropy alloy systems.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi‐principal element alloy (for example, an HEA such as the Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti system) in its disordered solid-solution state.
generation.intervention: Use the CALPHAD method combined with high-throughput calculations (HTC) to screen compositional space and predict phase stability and microstructural evolution under intended processing and operating conditions.
generation.conditions: Calculations performed over relevant composition ranges and temperatures (including processing and service conditions), ideally coupled with parallel computing resources to efficiently handle high computational loads.
generation.structural_mediator: The predicted stable primary solid-solution phase and any coherent precipitate phases (e.g., L2₁) that enhance strength, directly mediating microstructure refinement and property optimization.
generation.mechanism: CALPHAD employs thermodynamic databases and physicochemical criteria (such as mixing enthalpy, entropy, atomic size difference, and valence electron concentration) to predict phase diagrams. This enables the design of alloys with targeted phase stability and controlled precipitate formation that refines the microstructure and tailors mechanical/physical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys designed via this method are predicted to exhibit improved phase stability at operating temperatures, refined and homogeneous microstructures, and optimized combinations of mechanical and functional properties (strength, ductility, etc.) relative to alloys developed by traditional trial-and-error methods.
generation.baseline: Alloy design approaches relying solely on experimental trial and error without predictive thermodynamic modeling.
generation.boundary: The method’s effectiveness depends on the accuracy of the thermodynamic databases and the computational capacity available; complex multi-component systems may require further experimental validation.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative benefits of using CALPHAD-HTC are supported by current evidence, the exact quantitative improvements in phase stability and material properties remain system-dependent and require further study.

The design stage of the quinary HEA started with the calculation of the thermophysical parameters, mainly enthalpy of mixing (∆ H mix ), entropy of mixing ( Δ S mix ), atomic size difference ( δ ), and the omega parameter ( Ω ) for several compositions. The ability of a material to form a single-phase was empirically shown to depend on these three parameters. For that, the value for Δ H mix was recommended to be in the range of −15 to 5 kJ per mole, while δ should be smaller than 6.6 and Ω larger than 1.1 [26] , [27] . ∆ H mix , δ , and Ω were then calculated using Eqs. 1 – 4 respectively. Other theoretical parameters such as density ( ρ ), melting temperature ( T m ), and VEC were calculated using the rule of mixture, as shown in Eq. 5 , where i represents the element type, X represents the property, r is the atomic radius, and c represents the concentration of element i .

The atomic radii and enthalpy used in the calculations are taken from refs. [28] , [29] , respectively. The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

The computational software could significantly affect the efficiency of HTC since massive calculations are carried out. In the example of the Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system, it takes only a few hours on a desktop computer to finish the HTCs (~ 3 × 10 3 ) within the composition range of 5–50 at.% for each element and finally screen out eight potential alloys.
